title: Has the fast-paced and short-length social media entertainment influenced film pacing?

commenti.body: Oppenheimer was my first thought before you even mentioned it. You might be onto something, although it’s worth pointing out that a lot of Nolan’s movies follow a similar pace, going all the way back to Memento. Its not a major trend that I’ve noticed otherwise.

I think there’s a difference between fast-paced editing and films that are made to address people’s shorter attention span.

Here’s why I don’t think Oppenheimer could work with a different pace: Nolan made the decision to tell this story while following the events “realistically” – meaning a whole bunch of different people will be introduced and named, and the audience will need some sort of reminder when a character that was previously seen in a flash returns with another purpose (that’s why the cast is so huge). An old trope in biopic is simply to condense many people into a single character to make it easier for an audience to follow (Margot Robbie in Bombshell symbolizes a wide range of victims, but Charlize Theron and Nicole Kidman play real figures).

I liked your Oppenheimer example because, in this case, I believe it would be easier for Nolan to go the other way around if his concern was making a film for a social media conditioned audience. Quick scenes can be used to serve a complex narrative, not to "dumb it down" (for the lack of a better word). It varies, IMO.

>I just saw Oppenheimer and I expected to go into a beautifully shot slow paced film that went into the mind of a scientist that was at an ethical crossroads and instead I got what felt like 4 second scenes with quick cuts to the next and to the next and to the next, etc. with as much information as you can possibly handle in the shortest amount of time.

As someone else mentioned, I believe that specifically on Oppenheimer's case, it has to do more with Nolan's style rather than the media's influence—still, it would be interesting to analyse the audience reaction towards that style.

I've read some people say that the fast-paced rythym worked for such a dialogue-heavy movie, but that's such a... weird statement. I don't know exactly how to put it, but there has to be influence of fast-paced, short-length "content" you see in, let's say, social media, for someone to think that that's the way to deal with long biographic drama. And the cinematic aspect is left completely ignored, in my opinion, for a 3-hour montage of talking heads, medium-close-ups and vague to non-existent shot compositions—all so you can get... a Wikipedia article dictated by Matt Damon? I'm going off the rails though...

I believe you see more of this influence on more commercial movies. The ones you mentioned were directed by filmmakers with great artistic liberties, sl it's Nolan's style, Luhrmann—I mean, there's a chance though that just to seek for complacency they would adjust to trends of ways of entertainment. Or the producers would just force it.

If we are talking about movies made for Netflix or any other streaming platform which produces on mass, I would BELIEVE fast cuts and pacing are encouraged—these companies want to produce content (in the coldest definition of the word) to satisfy the consumer (cold), who influenced by the short-length entertainment in his daily life, will eventually want that speed, that fast/instant fulfillment too—it's content to consume.

At last, we can just try to analyse if the movie's speed is related to its themes.

Take Babylon for example (shit, I'll never shut up about this film), and the movie has so much speed you would think it's intended just for the new generations (it's a film about a subject no ones cares about though, yet is relevant). Blurry whip-pans, dolly zooms, long tracking shots and a fast rythym. This is a film about progress, the birth of an industry and of a new artform, the unhinged levels of creation and depravity in Hollywood, the wild, confusing, ruthless transition from silent to talkies, the rise and fall of artists, the sadness found once sober in a land of excess. It's a manic-depressive ride. Chazelle shows all of this confusion through an unforgiving pacing that constantly breaks and changes the tone of the film, that generates viewer the same confusion, adredaline and exhaustion that the characters and the world are going through.

Or let's take Everything Everywhere All At Once, a film that again captures so well the it's-all-too-much sensation we get in these confusing times for the world, where everything's advancing too fast and we never seem to adapt to the rythym of the modern life.

I had a similar thought when I saw Oppenheimer. 

However, I think Killer Of The Flower Moon and Priscilla, are examples where the director seems to knowingly fight against that influence. I enjoyed both of those films more too, but it was harder to get myself into the seat to watch the film (and to some extent reviews/box office also concur).

I definitely don’t think Nolan was in any way influenced by social media or anything of the sort. He’s an energetic action filmmaker and he brought that style to a biopic, to great effect I think. 

Elvis is pretty typical for Baz Luhrmann, his filmmaking style is breakneck and energetic (to a fault even) and part of what he’s trying to convey with the cinematography and editing of Elvis is the frantic, hectic life he led. 

I feel like I vaguely remember reading that the average shot length of Hollywood films has generally trended downwards over time, but we’re talking about since the 80s and 90s. You can look at something like the Saw films too, most of those movies are edited at an insanely frenetic pace and that was the early 2000s. 

I think subject matter more than style is often what conveys the zeitgeist a film is trying to capture though that’s a very broad statement.

In some ways yes, I do think so. But in a broader sense, I think it also comes down to competing with longer format storytelling as well. That standalone film is an inadequate medium to tell complex stories is a growing trend, even among intelligent and interested people. That in addition to emphasis on spectacle gives a certain weight to fast paced storytelling and editing. 

But to be fair, Nolan and Luhrman are also just the kind of filmmakers who naturally slot into those tendencies as it is, and while it was surprising for Oppenheimer, I more than expected and Elvis biopic to play out as such.

The first third of the movie felt like I was watching a series of trailers tbh. Really took me out of the movie. As others have pointed out though, this might've been just Christopher Nolan's style. He likes that kind of editing. I think it's to the detriment of the movie, though.

I think it's impacted individual films, but not films as a whole. There's been a lot of very spacey arthouse movies lately with plenty of long shots in them. It's only a few movies that kind of cater to that super short editing style, like Bullet Train or Babylon.

Yeah, if anything, Oppenheimer is the opposite. I'm a chemist, so I knew the majority of the historical figures in the film, and the context around their discoveries, so I loved the beginning. My friends who didn't found it boring and overlong.
Yeah, Baz Lurhmann doesn’t have fast paced editing because of social media and kids these days, he’s been making ultra fast paced editing since strictly ballroom in 1992.

Perhaps, but the rapid editing style reminiscent of MTV has consistently been a preferred approach for specific stories and directors. I am reminded of Oliver Stone's frenetic editing in the 90s, which transformed even a three-hour-long epic like "Nixon" into a visually challenging experience. This technique was even evident in Orson Welles' final and ultimately completed film, "The Other Side of the Wind."

> I definitely don’t think Nolan was in any way influenced by social media or anything of the sort.

Yes, I believe he specifically mentioned not being on any social media on the Fresh Air interview he did during the promotion for Oppenheimer.

I think the answer is definitely but also within the the industry practice as well.

Like I feel like somewhere between 2008 or 2010 it kind of became a thing where a normal blockbuster movie is two and a half hours long.. and I think that movies kind of are pulled in one direction of being longer, while at the same time catering to an audience of pretty much everyone, but in particular millennials and Gen Zs (with the infamous attention spans of 12 to  8 seconds.)

So I do think that the popular films are essentially breathless and kind of drawn out at the same time. 

If there's character development, it's usually tied to a plot twist. 

No Time to Die has Bond change life directions.. only for more complications to arise.

So what I think is the final effect is that audiences expect an action scene or a comedy scene with little to show how characters experience life or grow. 

Rise of Skywalker might be an infamous example of this -- the film never really stands still enough to let dramatic beats fall organically.  

So my belief is that different genres are more thoughtful with their pacing, but the general audience is kind of primed for this 'quick first act major event!"
